newTopics.title: Light & Shadow: Drawing Form
newTopics.summary: Every object turns from light into shadow. Learning to see that change is how a flat drawing becomes a solid form.
newTopics.tryIt: Put an apple or a mug under a single desk lamp. Squint, then shade only three values: light, middle and dark.

resources.title: The Silver Tureen
resources.creator: Jean Siméon Chardin, ca. 1728–30
resources.note: One soft light source — follow how it wraps around the round tureen and fruit.

resources.title: Chiaroscuro (Art Term)
resources.note: What chiaroscuro means: strong light and dark to create form and drama.

resources.title: Sketching is Seeing (6 short video activities)
resources.creator: Teaching artist Stephanie Morse
resources.note: Includes building a drawing from basic shapes and drawing negative space. For all ages.

newTopics.title: Perspective Basics: Horizon Line & Vanishing Point
newTopics.summary: Perspective makes a flat page feel deep. A horizon line, a vanishing point and a few guide lines are all you need to start.
keyConcepts: Orthogonals (lines that meet at the point)
newTopics.tryIt: Draw a long hallway or a street using one vanishing point. Then add a door on each side, all following the guide lines.

resources.title: How to draw The Met using perspective drawing | Drop-in Drawing
resources.note: Step-by-step: horizon line, vanishing points and drawing a real building.

resources.note: How Renaissance artists invented perspective, from Brunelleschi to Leonardo.

resources.title: The Draughtsman of the Lute
resources.creator: Albrecht Dürer, woodcut
resources.note: A 500-year-old 'perspective machine' — artists used string and a frame to plot points.

resources.title: How one-point linear perspective works
resources.creator: Dr. Beth Harris and Dr. Steven Zucker
resources.note: Essay and transcript to read alongside the video.

newTopics.title: Still Life: Learning from Everyday Objects
newTopics.summary: Artists have practiced on cups, fruit and bottles for centuries. Still life teaches shape, surface, light and arrangement all at once.
keyConcepts: Looking at the gaps between things
newTopics.tryIt: Choose three objects of different heights and textures. Arrange them three different ways and do a quick thumbnail of each before picking your favorite.

resources.title: The Basket of Apples
resources.creator: Paul Cezanne, c. 1893
resources.note: Look closely: the table edges don't line up. Cezanne bent the rules to balance the picture.

resources.title: Still-Life Painting in Northern Europe, 1600–1800
resources.creator: Walter A. Liedtke
resources.note: How Dutch painters turned flowers, food and silver into a whole art form.

newTopics.title: Gesture & Movement: Drawing Figures in Action
newTopics.summary: Gesture drawing captures the energy of a pose in seconds — the line of action first, details later.
keyConcepts: Drawing what moves, not what's still
newTopics.tryIt: Ask someone to hold five different poses for 30 seconds each. Draw only one flowing line for each pose before adding anything else.

resources.title: Two Dancers
resources.creator: Edgar Degas, c. 1893–98 (pastel and charcoal)
resources.note: Degas drew dancers again and again to catch balance and movement.

resources.title: How to Sketch Movement | Drop-in Drawing
resources.note: Short demonstration of sketching figures in motion.

resources.title: Sketching is Seeing: one-line and less-dominant-hand drawing
resources.creator: Teaching artist Stephanie Morse
resources.note: Loosening-up exercises that train fast, confident lines.

newTopics.title: Portrait Drawing: Seeing a Face
newTopics.summary: A good portrait starts with big shapes and placement — where the eyes, nose and mouth sit — before any detail.
keyConcepts: The egg shape of the head
Light and planes of the face
newTopics.tryIt: Draw a friend's portrait in 10 lines or fewer. Then draw it again with as many lines as you like. Which one feels more like them?

resources.title: Madame Guillaume Guillon Lethière and her son Lucien
resources.creator: Jean Auguste Dominique Ingres, 1808 (graphite)
resources.note: Pencil only: careful faces, quick clothing — notice where Ingres spends his detail.

resources.title: Sketching is Seeing: a portrait in 10 lines or fewer
resources.creator: Teaching artist Stephanie Morse
resources.note: A playful exercise in finding the most important lines of a face.

newTopics.title: Landscape: Painting Outdoors and the Oil Sketch
newTopics.summary: Painting outdoors (plein air) trains you to see light and atmosphere quickly. Many great landscapes began as small, fast sketches.
keyConcepts: Atmosphere: far things look paler and cooler
Working fast while the light changes
newTopics.tryIt: Go outside for 15 minutes. Paint or draw only three big shapes — sky, ground, one main object — with no details at all.

resources.title: Landscape

resources.note: Soft, silvery tones — Corot simplifies trees into big masses of light and dark.
